reason: A six-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse. “in the name of Jesus” is the King James formula for apostolic action and 4 Nephi 1:1 and 1:5 use it as such — baptized in the name of Jesus, miracles worked in nothing save the name of Jesus. sharedText: rich and poor ... free and bond
reason: A tempting entry and it has to be written out, because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. 4 Nephi 1:3 abolishes two social pairs in one clause — 'there were not rich and poor, bond and free' — and the King James Bible pairs those same two pairs in exactly one verse: “rich and poor” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and Revelation 13:16 is the only one that continues 'free and bond'. But the order is inverted (the Book of Mormon's own “bond and free” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses), the context is opposed at the only point that matters — Revelation enumerates the categories in order to say the beast marks every one of them, 4 Nephi enumerates them in order to say they ceased to exist — and Revelation 13:16's actual subject, the mark in the right hand or forehead, has no counterpart here. The idea's real King James home is Galatians 3:28, where “bond nor free” is abolished and 'ye are all one in Christ Jesus'; that verse is recorded as a composite on the Acts 4:32 row and its 'all one' resurfaces at 1:17.

Typology pulls hard and the wording will not quite bear it. A covenant people multiplying rapidly in a land after a deliverance is Exodus 1:7 — 'the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty' — and 4 Nephi 1:10 reads 'did wax strong, and did multiply exceeding fast'. The elements are all there and none of them is contiguous: “waxed exceeding” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 1:7 and Daniel 8:9, and the Book of Mormon has neither, splitting 'wax' onto 'strong' and 'exceeding' onto 'fast'. tools/mediation-check.py was run against the New Testament form, Acts 7:17 ('the people grew and multiplied in Egypt'), and returned one decisive point for Exodus on the strength of 'waxed exceeding' — but that is the very phrase the Book of Mormon does not reproduce, so the verdict decides between two candidates neither of which is demonstrably present. Recorded so that a reader who sees the Exodus pattern is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

The model case for this category in the chapter. “fasting and prayer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 4 Nephi 1:12 has it exactly: 'continuing in fasting and prayer'. A singleton match on a devotional phrase in a devotional verse looks decisive until the source verse is read. 1 Corinthians 7:5 is Paul on conjugal duty — 'Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.' The phrase names a temporary abstention from marriage, and 'come together again' in that verse means resuming it. 4 Nephi 1:12 uses the same three words for a congregation's ordinary devotion and then says they were 'meeting together oft'. The collocation of fasting with prayer is unavoidable in English and the Book of Mormon uses it throughout; the singleton is an accident of the KJV's preferring 'prayer and fasting' everywhere else.

A five-word run made entirely of articles, a preposition and 'people'. Esther 3:8 is Haman denouncing a scattered people to Ahasuerus; 4 Nephi 1:13 is a peace notice. Nothing content-bearing is shared.

The machine's proposal for the verse, on a four-word run, and it is superseded. “the love of God” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses, so the phrase alone points nowhere; what the Book of Mormon adds is the verb, and “dwelleth the love of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:17, where the love of God dwelling in a man is tested by whether he shares his goods with a brother in need. Romans 8:39's love of God is the love from which nothing can separate us — a different proposition, in a different grammatical relation, with no dwelling in it. The link is written at this verse to 1 John 3:17.

sharedText: passed away and there was no
reason: A six-word run and the highest-scoring candidate for the verse, and it is an artifact of two independent formulas colliding. 4 Nephi dates every paragraph by years that pass away and denies contention in every one of its golden-age verses, so 'passed away, and there was no contention' is simply those two habits meeting. Revelation 21:1's 'were passed away; and there was no more sea' is the dissolution of the first heaven and the first earth. The senses are not merely different but incompatible: in Revelation the passing away is the end of the old order and the beginning of the new, in 4 Nephi it is the calendar. Worth the entry because 4 Nephi 1:18 is also the verse in which the first generation from Christ passes away, which makes the eschatological reading momentarily attractive.

“get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13, and 4 Nephi 1:26's 'churches unto themselves, to get gain' will attract the candidate. James 4:13 is about merchants presuming on tomorrow, and the Book of Mormon uses 'get gain' as a fixed idiom for priestcraft from 2 Nephi 26:29 onward. A reader of this verse is sent to Alma 11:20.

Leviticus 6:5 is restitution law — restoring a thing 'unto him to whom it appertaineth' — and 4 Nephi 1:27 is about administering what is sacred 'unto him to whom it had been forbidden'. The two clauses are opposite in force, one about restoring property to its owner and one about giving holy things to a man debarred from them, and share no content word.

The catalogue therefore declines to press the John 12:40 contact and says so on the link at this verse: mediation for the hardening clause specifically is left undecided rather than resolved by the company it keeps.

A four-word run and pure numeral. 4 Nephi dates by years from the coming of Christ in almost every verse, and 'three hundred and five' happens to coincide with the first four words of Daniel 12:12's 'thousand three hundred and five and thirty days'. The parallel is arithmetic, and the same reasoning was filed against 1 Chronicles 26:31 at Helaman 1:1. This entry covers every regnal- or year-numeral candidate in the chapter.

'Ammaron, being constrained by the Holy Ghost' invites two candidates and takes neither. “constraineth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Job 32:18, 'the spirit within me constraineth me', which is Elihu compelled to speak, and 2 Corinthians 5:14, 'the love of Christ constraineth us'. Job's is the closer, pairing a spirit with the verb, but the Book of Mormon's participle is passive where Job's verb is active, the constraint in Job is toward speech where Ammaron's is toward concealment, and the corpus uses 'constrained by the Spirit' as its own idiom elsewhere. Two words in a different voice and an opposed action.
